title: Cognitive Set 03: Combinatorics, Clocks & Logic
description: Challenging set featuring circular tracks, half-yearly CI, 3-set Venn diagrams, campus funnel DI, coded relations, and critical verbal reasoning.

questions.question: Two runners A and B start simultaneously from the same point on a 1,200-metre circular track and run in the same direction at constant speeds of 6 m/s and 4 m/s respectively. After how many minutes will they meet at the starting point together for the first time?
questions.explanation: Time for A to complete 1 lap = 1200 / 6 = 200 seconds. Time for B to complete 1 lap = 1200 / 4 = 300 seconds. Both return to the starting point together at LCM(200, 300) = 600 seconds = 10 minutes.
questions.shortcut: Meet at START = LCM(lap time A, lap time B) = LCM(200s, 300s) = 600s = 10 min.

questions.question: A sum of Rs. 16,000 is invested at 10% per annum compound interest, compounded half-yearly, for 1.5 years. What is the compound interest earned?
If alpha and beta are the roots of the quadratic equation x^2 - 7x + 10 = 0, what is the value of alpha^3 + beta^3?
questions.explanation: Sum of roots (alpha + beta) = 7 and product (alpha * beta) = 10. Using alpha^3 + beta^3 = (alpha + beta)^3 - 3*alpha*beta*(alpha + beta) = 343 - 3*10*7 = 343 - 210 = 133.
questions.shortcut: Roots factor cleanly to 2 and 5: 2^3 + 5^3 = 8 + 125 = 133.

questions.question: In a batch of 120 trainees, 70 know Java, 60 know SQL, and 50 know Python. Thirty know both Java and SQL, 25 know SQL and Python, 20 know Java and Python, and 10 know all three languages. How many trainees know NONE of the three languages?
questions.explanation: By inclusion-exclusion, |J u S u P| = 70 + 60 + 50 - (30 + 25 + 20) + 10 = 180 - 75 + 10 = 115. Trainees knowing none = 120 - 115 = 5.

questions.question: A right-angled triangle has perpendicular sides of lengths 9 cm and 12 cm. What is the area of the circle inscribed inside this triangle?
questions.explanation: Hypotenuse c = sqrt(9^2 + 12^2) = 15 cm. Inradius of a right triangle r = (a + b - c)/2 = (9 + 12 - 15)/2 = 3 cm. Area of inscribed circle = pi * r^2 = 9*pi sq cm.
questions.shortcut: Right-triangle inradius r = (a + b - c)/2 = (9+12-15)/2 = 3 => Area = 9*pi.

questions.passage:
Campus Hiring Funnel Across 4 Colleges:
- College A: 400 Applied | 160 Cleared Ascend | 48 Selected
- College B: 500 Applied | 225 Cleared Ascend | 54 Selected
- College C: 300 Applied | 105 Cleared Ascend | 42 Selected
- College D: 600 Applied | 210 Cleared Ascend | 63 Selected
questions.question: Which college recorded the highest conversion percentage from 'Cleared Ascend' to 'Selected'?
questions.explanation: Conversion rates: A = 48/160 = 30%; B = 54/225 = 24%; C = 42/105 = 40%; D = 63/210 = 30%. College C is highest at 40%.
questions.shortcut: Check ratios: 42/105 = 2/5 = 40%, higher than 30% (A, D) and 24% (B).

Eight friends J, K, L, M, N, O, P, and Q sit around a square table: four at the corners facing outward and four at the midpoints of the sides facing inward. K sits at a corner and is second to the right of J. M sits immediately right of K and faces O. L sits immediately to the right of O. N sits at a midpoint and is not adjacent to M. P sits opposite N. Who sits immediately to the right of Q?
questions.explanation: Number seats 1..8 clockwise: odd {1,3,5,7} are corners facing OUT (right = +1 clockwise); even {2,4,6,8} are midpoints facing IN (right = -1 counter-clockwise). Set K=1 (corner). K is 2nd right of J => J=7 (7->8->1). M is immediately right of K(1) => M=2, facing O=6. L is immediately right of O(6, facing IN, right=-1) => L=5. N is at a midpoint not adjacent to M(2), so N=4, and opposite P=8. Remaining corner seat 3 is Q. Immediately right of Q(3, facing OUT, right=+1) is seat 4 = N.
questions.shortcut: Clockwise 1..8 (odd=corner out, even=side in): [1:K, 2:M, 3:Q, 4:N, 5:L, 6:O, 7:J, 8:P] => right of Q(3) is N(4).

questions.question: Statements: (1) Some threads are deadlocked. (2) No deadlocked item is preemptible. (3) Some preemptible items are prioritized. Conclusions: I. All threads are prioritized. II. Some threads are not prioritized.
options: Either Conclusion I or II follows
Neither Conclusion I nor II follows
questions.explanation: There is no direct constraint forcing all threads into prioritized or excluding all threads from prioritized. Because 'All A are B' and 'Some A are not B' form a universal-particular complementary pair with identical subject ('threads') and predicate ('prioritized'), either I or II must hold.
questions.shortcut: Complementary pair 'All X are Y' + 'Some X are not Y' with no definite link => Either I or II.

questions.question: D is the daughter of E. F is the brother of D. G is the wife of E. H is the mother of G. If E has only one son, how is F related to H?
questions.explanation: D is E's daughter and F is D's brother, so F is E's son. G is E's wife, so G is F's mother. H is G's mother, making H the maternal grandmother of F. Thus F is H's grandson.
questions.shortcut: F = son of (E, G); H = mother of G => F is H's grandson.

questions.question: If A=1, B=2, ..., Z=26, and in a code JAVA is written as 68 and CODE is written as 54, how is NODE written in the same code? (Verify: sum of positions * 2! JAVA: 10+1+22+1=34 * 2 = 68; CODE: 3+15+4+5=27 * 2 = 54; NODE: 14+15+4+5=38 * 2 = 76.)
questions.explanation: Each word is coded as 2 * (sum of alphabetical positions of its letters). JAVA = 2*(10+1+22+1) = 68. CODE = 2*(3+15+4+5) = 54. NODE = 2*(14+15+4+5) = 2*38 = 76.
questions.shortcut: Sum letter ranks (14+15+4+5 = 38) and double it => 76.

questions.question: Statements: M >= N = O > P; Q <= P < R; S > M. Conclusions: I. S > P. II. N > Q. III. R > M.
options: All I, II, and III follow
questions.explanation: S > M >= N = O > P => S > P (I follows). N = O > P >= Q => N > Q (II follows). Between R and M, R > P < O <= M gives opposite signs, so R > M cannot be concluded (III fails).
questions.shortcut: I: S > M >= O > P (valid); II: N = O > P >= Q (valid); III: opposite signs between R and M.

questions.question: Find the next term in the series: 3, 10, 29, 66, 127, ?
In triangle ABC, what is the measure of angle B? Statement I: AB = BC and angle A = 50 degrees. Statement II: Exterior angle at C is 130 degrees.
options: Either Statement I alone or Statement II alone is sufficient
questions.explanation: From Statement I: Since AB = BC, angles opposite them are equal, so angle C = angle A = 50 degrees. Thus angle B = 180 - 50 - 50 = 80 degrees (sufficient). Statement II only gives interior angle C = 180 - 130 = 50 degrees, leaving angles A and B undetermined (insufficient).
questions.shortcut: Isosceles base angle A=50 gives C=50 and B=80 uniquely from I alone.

questions.question: A technician walks 15 m East from server rack A, turns right and walks 8 m, turns left and walks 9 m, and finally turns left and walks 15 m to reach rack B. What is the straight-line distance between rack A and rack B?
questions.explanation: Track coordinates from (0,0): +15 East => (15,0); right (South) 8 => (15,-8); left (East) 9 => (24,-8); left (North) 15 => (24,7). Straight-line distance = sqrt(24^2 + 7^2) = sqrt(576 + 49) = sqrt(625) = 25 m.
questions.shortcut: Net East = 15+9 = 24, Net North = 15-8 = 7; (7, 24, 25) Pythagorean triple!

questions.question: A 4-member incident response team must be selected from programmers {A, B, C, D} and SREs {W, X, Y, Z} with at least 2 SREs. A and W cannot serve together. D refuses to serve if A serves. X and Z cannot serve together. If B is chosen, X must be chosen. Y refuses to serve unless C is also chosen. If both A and Z are selected, who else MUST be on the team?
questions.explanation: With A and Z on the team: A excludes W and D; Z excludes X. Since X is excluded, B cannot be chosen. We still need 2 more members with at least 1 more SRE from {W, X, Y}. Only Y is available as the second SRE, and Y requires C. Thus the unique team is {A, C, Y, Z}, so C and Y must join.
questions.shortcut: A blocks W,D; Z blocks X (which blocks B) => only C and Y remain.

questions.question: Fact: Every database table in Module X that uses a composite primary key also has a foreign key constraint. Fact: No table in Module X with a foreign key constraint allows unindexed deletes. Which conclusion MUST be true?
options: Every table in Module X that disallows unindexed deletes has a composite primary key
No table in Module X with a composite primary key allows unindexed deletes
Some tables in Module X have neither a primary key nor a foreign key
All tables in Module X use composite primary keys
questions.explanation: Chain of implications in Module X: Composite PK => Foreign Key => Disallows unindexed deletes. Therefore, no table in Module X with a composite primary key can allow unindexed deletes.
questions.shortcut: All A are B, No B is C => No A is C.

questions.passage: Edge computing shifts latency-sensitive inference closer to sensors rather than hauling raw video or telemetry streams back to centralized cloud regions. On factory floors, shaving forty milliseconds off defect-detection loops determines whether a robotic arm diverts a flawed component before assembly continues. Yet decentralization introduces a quieter operational burden: instead of patching ten monolithic servers in a controlled data center, fleet operators must orchestrate cryptographically signed updates across thousands of intermittently connected gateways running on heterogeneous hardware.
questions.question: According to the passage, what is the primary operational challenge introduced by edge computing?
options: Robotic arms respond too slowly to centralized cloud alerts
Managing secure software updates across numerous, varied, and intermittently online field devices
Raw video streams cannot be encrypted before reaching factory gateways
Centralized cloud regions lack sufficient compute capacity for telemetry
questions.explanation: The final sentence identifies the operational burden as orchestrating cryptographically signed updates across thousands of intermittently connected, heterogeneous gateways.
questions.shortcut: Read after 'Yet decentralization introduces a quieter operational burden:'.

questions.passage: Edge computing shifts latency-sensitive inference closer to sensors rather than hauling raw video or telemetry streams back to centralized cloud regions. On factory floors, shaving forty milliseconds off defect-detection loops determines whether a robotic arm diverts a flawed component before assembly continues. Yet decentralization introduces a quieter operational burden: instead of patching ten monolithic servers in a controlled data center, fleet operators must orchestrate cryptographically signed updates across thousands of intermittently connected gateways running on heterogeneous hardware.
questions.question: In the context of the passage, the word 'heterogeneous' most nearly means:
questions.explanation: 'Heterogeneous hardware' contrasts with controlled homogeneous data-center servers, meaning varied or diverse device models and architectures.
questions.shortcut: Hetero = different/diverse; contrasts with 'controlled data center' servers.

questions.question: Identify the erroneous part: 'By the time the overnight batch job finishes, (A) / the reporting warehouse will already ingested (B) / nearly four million transaction records (C) / from the regional payment gateways. (D)'
questions.explanation: Future perfect tense requires 'will have + past participle': segment (B) should be 'will already have ingested', not 'will already ingested'.
questions.shortcut: Missing auxiliary 'have' after 'will already' before past participle 'ingested'.

questions.question:
Arrange P, Q, R, S into a coherent paragraph:
P. Without idempotency keys, a harmless client retry after a brief network timeout can charge a customer's card twice.
Q. Distributed payment APIs frequently encounter transient packet drops between mobile clients and backend gateways.
R. Assigning a unique key to each logical checkout attempt lets the server safely deduplicate repeated requests.
S. Consequently, modern fintech architectures treat idempotency as a mandatory correctness guarantee rather than an optional optimization.
questions.explanation: Q introduces transient network drops. P explains the risk of retries ('charge twice'). R presents the solution ('idempotency keys' / unique key). S draws the closing principle ('Consequently'). Order: Q-P-R-S.
questions.shortcut: Problem (Q) -> Risk without fix (P) -> Fix (R) -> Conclusion (S).

questions.question: Choose the cleanest replacement: 'The throughput of the new connection pool is nearly double [the legacy JDBC driver].'
options: that of the legacy JDBC driver
what the legacy JDBC driver was
questions.explanation: You must compare like with like: 'throughput' cannot be compared directly to 'driver'; use the demonstrative pronoun 'that' ('that of the legacy JDBC driver') to stand for 'the throughput'.
questions.shortcut: Compare 'throughput' with 'that [throughput] of the legacy JDBC driver'.

questions.question: Select the best pair: 'Far from being ______ to junior engineers, the architect's blunt code reviews were prized for their ______ clarity.'
questions.explanation: 'Far from being X' contrasts with 'prized for Y'. 'Demoralizing' fits the feared negative reaction to blunt reviews, while 'incisive' (sharp, clear) explains why they were prized.
questions.shortcut: 'Far from being [negative]' contrasts with 'prized for [positive]'.

questions.question: Find the erroneous segment: 'The sprint retrospective discussed about (A) / automating smoke tests (B) / prior to every weekly release (C) / across all customer portals. (D)'
questions.explanation: 'Discuss' is a transitive verb and does not take 'about' after it. Segment (A) should simply say 'discussed automating smoke tests'.
questions.shortcut: Never use 'discuss about'; 'discuss' takes a direct object.

questions.question:
Order P, Q, R, S logically:
P. Yet relying exclusively on end-to-end browser tests slows feedback loops to a crawl and flakes under minor UI tweaks.
Q. Automated testing suites safeguard software reliability as codebases scale.
R. Combining fast unit tests at the base with targeted integration checks balances speed with confidence.
S. A single UI selector change can fail dozens of suites even when core business logic remains intact.
questions.explanation: Q introduces automated suites. P introduces the limitation of over-relying on E2E tests. S illustrates why ('flakes under minor UI tweaks' -> 'A single UI selector change'). R offers the balanced solution. Order: Q-P-S-R.
questions.shortcut: P mentions 'flakes under minor UI tweaks', and S immediately exemplifies 'A single UI selector change'.

questions.question: Pick the correct improvement: 'Switching to prepared statements resulted in [less SQL parsing errors] and tighter memory bounds.'
questions.explanation: 'Errors' is a plural countable noun, which requires 'fewer' rather than 'less' (used for uncountable quantities).
questions.shortcut: Countable plural ('errors') => 'fewer'; uncountable ('latency') => 'less'.

questions.question: Passage: 'During a code audit, every module with cyclomatic complexity above 20 exhibited at least three production defects last year, whereas 80% of modules with complexity under 10 had zero defects.' Which conclusion is strictly supported?
options: Lowering a module's cyclomatic complexity below 10 guarantees zero production defects
No module with cyclomatic complexity above 20 had fewer than three production defects last year
20% of all modules in the codebase had high cyclomatic complexity
High cyclomatic complexity is the sole cause of production defects
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states that 'every module with cyclomatic complexity above 20 exhibited at least three production defects last year', which logically entails that none of those modules had fewer than three defects.
questions.shortcut: 'Every X had >= 3' directly translates to 'No X had < 3'.
